title: Are Facebook Ads Worth It for Contractors in 2026?
desc: Are Facebook ads worth it for contractors? 2026 cost per lead figures, a break even sum, lead forms vs calls, housing ad rules and a one month test plan.

blocks.h1: Are Facebook ads worth it for contractors, *or just a money pit?*
blocks.lede: Facebook ads are worth it for contractors when your jobs are big enough to absorb a lead cost of around $40 to $50, you can call every lead back within minutes, and you have real photos of your work. They are usually not worth it for small, urgent jobs, where people search Google instead of scrolling. Run the break even sum below before you spend a cent, then test for one month with a fixed budget.
ticks: What Facebook leads cost in 2026, and the sum that tells you if they pay
Lead forms versus calls, and how to cut out the tyre kickers
A one month test plan, ad text to copy and a follow up script

blocks.html:
Are Facebook ads worth it for contractors?

Sometimes, yes. Facebook ads (Meta ads, which also run on Instagram) work for some trades and burn money for others. The difference is not luck. It comes down to four things:

  • Job size. Remodels, kitchens, bathrooms, roofs, decks, driveways, solar, landscaping projects and HVAC replacements can pay back a $40 lead easily. A $150 tap repair cannot.
  • How people buy. Nobody scrolls Instagram while their pipe is bursting. They search Google. Facebook shows your ad to people who were not looking yet, so it suits planned projects, not emergencies.
  • Speed. A Facebook lead is a person who tapped a button between videos. If you call in five minutes they remember you. If you call tomorrow, many will not.
  • Proof. Real before and after photos, short clips from site and good reviews do the selling. Stock photos of smiling families do not.

If you tick all four, Facebook can be a steady source of work, especially for filling the diary weeks ahead. If you mainly do small or emergency jobs, put your money into your Google Business Profile, reviews and Google ads first. Our guide to whether Local Services Ads are worth it covers the Google side.

How much do Facebook ads cost for contractors in 2026?

WordStream's 2026 Facebook ads benchmarks, published in September 2026 and based on campaigns run between April 2025 and June 2026, give these averages for the Home and Home Improvement category:

MeasureHome and Home ImprovementAll industries
Cost per lead (lead campaigns)$42.95$27.39
Conversion rate (lead campaigns)5.32%8.54%
Cost per click (lead campaigns)$2.18$1.80
Cost per click (traffic campaigns)$0.63$0.60

So home improvement leads cost more than average and convert worse than average. That is normal: a new kitchen is a bigger decision than a pizza. The figures are in US dollars and are averages, so your area, trade and ads could land well above or below them.

On budgets, software firm JobNimbus suggests in a 2026 roofing guide that smaller and newer firms usually start between $500 and $1,500 a month, or $20 to $40 a day while the ads learn. That is a sensible range for most trades testing it for the first time. Below about $10 a day, it takes a long time to collect enough leads to judge anything.

How do you know if Facebook ads will pay for you?

Do this sum before you spend anything. It tells you the most you can afford to pay for one lead.

Maximum cost per lead = average profit per job x the share of leads that become jobs

Here is a worked example with round numbers. Swap in your own.

StepExample
Monthly budget$1,000
Leads at about $43 each1,000 / 43 = about 23 leads
Leads you actually reach (say 70%)about 16 conversations
Conversations that lead to a quote (say half)8 quotes
Quotes you win (say 1 in 4)2 jobs
Profit per job on a $6,000 job at 30% margin$1,800
Profit from the month2 x 1,800 = $3,600, against $1,000 spent

In this example, 2 jobs from 23 leads means roughly 1 job per 12 leads. So the most you could pay per lead and still break even is $1,800 / 12 = $150. At $43 a lead there is plenty of room.

Now run it for a handyman type job worth $400 with $120 profit. The same 2 jobs bring $240 profit for $1,000 of ads. That is why Facebook suits bigger tickets. The percentages above are examples for the sum, not promises; track your own for a month and use those.

Lead forms, calls or your website: which is best?

Meta gives you three main ways to collect enquiries. Each has a trade off.

  • Instant forms (lead ads). The person taps the ad and a form opens inside Facebook with their name, phone and email already filled in. This gives the cheapest leads and the most of them, and it is also where most of the complaints about tyre kickers (tire kickers in the USA) come from, because sending the form takes two taps.
  • Call ads. The button rings your phone. Fewer enquiries, but each one is a real conversation. Only use this if someone answers during the hours the ad runs.
  • Traffic to your website. Clicks are cheaper, but the person has to fill in your own form. Fewer leads, usually better ones, and only worth it if your site loads fast on a phone and has a clear quote form. See what a trade website needs.

Most trades start with instant forms, then tighten them using the steps below. If the leads are still poor after that, test sending people to a page on your website instead.

How do you stop getting junk leads from Facebook?

Trades on owner forums report the same problems again and again: people who do not remember filling in the form, wrong numbers, people outside the area, and people who only wanted a rough price. You will never remove all of them, but you can cut them a lot.

  • Choose the higher intent form type. When you build an instant form, Meta lets you pick a form type made for volume or one made for higher intent, which adds a review step before sending. Pick higher intent. You get fewer leads, but more of them are real.
  • Add two or three qualifying questions. For example: "What is the project?" (multiple choice), "When are you hoping to start?" and "What is your postcode or ZIP code?" Each question removes some casual tappers.
  • Put the price range in the ad. "Most bathroom refits we do are between $X and $Y" puts off people expecting a bargain. Use your real typical range.
  • Show your own work. Before and after photos from real local jobs, with the suburb or town named.
  • Call within five minutes. This matters more than any setting. A lead called the next day often goes cold.
  • Tell Meta which leads were good. If you use a CRM that connects to Meta, mark leads that turned into quotes and jobs, so the system finds more people like them.

Our guide on how to deal with time wasters has more ways to filter enquiries before you drive out to quote.

Are there special rules for contractor ads on Facebook?

Yes, and they catch a lot of trades out. Meta has a Housing special ad category, and its list of what counts includes housing repairs as well as things like home sales, rentals and home insurance. Meta applies it to advertisers in the USA and to ads aimed at people in the USA, Canada and certain parts of Europe. If your ad is for home repair or improvement work, you may need to declare it, and Meta can reject or limit ads that should have been declared.

When the Housing category applies, the targeting limits include:

  • Age stays at 18 to 65+ and cannot be narrowed.
  • Gender stays at all genders.
  • Location must cover at least a 15 mile radius around any point you pick, and you cannot target by postcode or ZIP code.
  • Lookalike and saved audiences are not available, and you cannot exclude detailed targeting options.

In practice, this means the old advice to "target homeowners aged 35 to 54 in these three ZIP codes" often cannot be followed. Your ad text and photos have to do the filtering instead, which is another reason to name your area and your price range in the ad. Check what Ads Manager asks for when you set up the campaign, and read Meta's own help page on ads for housing if you are unsure.

What should a contractor Facebook ad say?

Keep it plain and specific. Here are three you can adapt. Change the town, the job and the numbers to your own.

1. Planned project

"We have just finished this bathroom refit in [town]. New tiles, walk in shower, heated rail, done in eight working days. We are booking projects for [month] now. Most of our bathrooms come in between $X and $Y. Tap below to get a quote, and we will call you back the same day."

2. Seasonal offer

"Winter is the time to get your spring deck booked. We are taking [number] more deck builds in [area] for [month]. Fixed written quotes, photos of every job on our page. Tap below and tell us roughly what you have in mind."

3. Free check, for roofing, gutters or HVAC

"Not sure if your roof made it through the last storm? We are doing free roof checks in [area] this month. Photos of anything we find, no pressure to book. Tap below to pick a time."

Use one real photo or a short phone video from the job. Clips of the work in progress usually look more trustworthy than polished graphics.

What should you say when you call a Facebook lead?

Call first. If there is no answer, send a text straight away, because many people will not pick up an unknown number. Copy these:

Call script: "Hi [Name], it is [your name] from [business]. You asked about [project] on Facebook a few minutes ago, so I thought I would give you a quick ring. Have you got two minutes? What are you hoping to get done, and roughly when?"

Text if they do not answer: "Hi [Name], it is [your name] from [business]. Thanks for asking about [project] on Facebook. I tried to call. When is a good time for a quick chat? Or reply here with a few photos and I can give you a rough idea."

Second text, the next day: "Hi [Name], just checking you saw my message about your [project]. Happy to help whenever suits. If you have already sorted it, no problem at all."

After that, stop. Mark the lead as dead in your spreadsheet or CRM so your numbers stay honest.

How do you test Facebook ads without wasting money?

Treat the first month as a test with a fixed limit.

  1. Set the budget. Pick a monthly amount you can afford to lose, for example $600 to $1,000, and set it as the campaign limit.
  2. One campaign, one service. Advertise your most profitable job, not everything you do.
  3. Two or three ads. Different photos, same offer. Let Meta show the one that works.
  4. Higher intent instant form with your qualifying questions.
  5. Leave it alone for at least a week. Big daily changes restart the learning. If it works, raise the budget by around 20% to 30% at a time, as JobNimbus advises.
  6. Track every lead in a simple sheet: date, name, reached or not, quoted or not, won or not, job value.
  7. Judge it on jobs, not leads. At the end of the month, compare profit from won jobs with the spend. Remember that some quotes will close later, so check again a month after.

If the numbers work, keep going and widen it slowly. If they do not, the problem is usually the offer, the photos or the follow up speed, rather than Facebook itself. Fix one thing and test again. If it still fails, put the money into reviews and your Google profile. The Google reviews guide is a good place to start, and strong reviews make your Facebook ads work better too, because people check you out before they reply.

blocks.title: Your checklist.
items: Run the break even sum with your own job value, margin and win rate
Pick one profitable, planned service to advertise
Set a fixed monthly test budget you can afford to lose
Use real photos of local jobs and name your area and price range
Choose the higher intent instant form and add two or three qualifying questions
Check whether the Housing special ad category applies to your ads
Call every lead within five minutes and text if they do not answer
Track every lead to a won or lost job and judge the month on profit

items.q: How much should a contractor spend on Facebook ads?
items.a: Many small firms start with $500 to $1,500 a month, or $20 to $40 a day, which is the range JobNimbus suggests in its 2026 roofing guide. Start with an amount you can afford to lose for a month and judge it on jobs won.

items.q: What is a good cost per lead on Facebook for contractors?
items.a: WordStream's 2026 benchmarks put the average for home and home improvement lead campaigns at $42.95. A good cost per lead for you is anything below your own break even figure: profit per job multiplied by the share of leads that become jobs.

items.q: Why are my Facebook leads so bad?
items.a: Usually because the form is too easy to send, the ad does not mention your area or price range, or the leads are called back too slowly. Switch to a higher intent form, add qualifying questions and call within five minutes.

items.q: Are Facebook ads or Google ads better for contractors?
items.a: Google is usually better for urgent and emergency work, because people search when they need someone now. Facebook is better for planned projects like remodels, decks and roofs, where you can catch people before they start searching.

items.q: Do I need a website to run Facebook ads?
items.a: Not for instant form or call ads, which keep people inside Facebook. But most people will look you up before they reply, so a fast website with real project photos and reviews makes the leads you pay for more likely to turn into jobs.

items.q: Can I target homeowners only on Facebook?
items.a: Often not directly. If your ads fall in Meta's Housing special ad category, you cannot narrow by age, gender or ZIP code and lookalike audiences are not available. Use your ad text, photos and qualifying questions to attract the right people instead.
